abstract: |
  **Background.** Game-based teaching strategies — gamification, game-based learning (GBL),
  and serious games — are increasingly used in nursing education, but their pooled effect
  on learning outcomes across the New World Kirkpatrick Model (NWKM) levels is unclear.
  **Objective.** To systematically review randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing
  game-based teaching with conventional teaching in nursing learners, and to meta-analyse
  effects on learning outcomes.
  **Methods.** PubMed, Scopus, and Europe PMC were searched from inception to May 2026
  (CINAHL, Embase, ERIC, PsycINFO, Cochrane, and Chinese databases are pending).
  Eligible studies were RCTs/cluster-RCTs of game-based teaching versus non-game conventional
  teaching in nursing students, interns, clinical nurses, or nursing teachers, reporting a
  quantitative learning/teaching outcome. Screening, eligibility assessment, dimension
  coding, RoB 2, and GRADE were performed with an AI-assisted pipeline (single reviewer,
  abstract-based). Standardized mean differences (Hedges' g) for L2 (knowledge/skill)
  outcomes were pooled with a DerSimonian–Laird random-effects model.
  **Results.** Of 640 records (315 after de-duplication), 88 studies were provisionally
  eligible (61 RCTs confirmed from abstract; 27 pending full-text confirmation); 5 contributed
  extractable group statistics. Pooled effect on L2 outcomes favoured game-based teaching
  (g = 0.65, 95% CI 0.24–1.05; p = 0.002) with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 71%); the
  95% prediction interval (−0.72 to 2.01) crossed the null. GRADE certainty was Low to Very low.
  **Conclusion.** Available RCT evidence suggests a moderate positive effect of game-based
  teaching on nursing learners' knowledge and skills, but heterogeneity and low certainty
  temper this. **This report is an automated, abstract-derived synthesis intended for review;
  full-text extraction and dual human verification are required before submission.**

# Introduction

Nursing education must build knowledge, psychomotor skill, clinical reasoning, and
professional confidence under increasing curricular and clinical-placement constraints.
Game-based teaching strategies — **gamification** (points, badges, leaderboards, levels,
rewards, competition), **game-based learning (GBL)**, and **serious games** (purpose-built
games with narrative/role/decision architecture) — are widely promoted as engaging,
active-learning alternatives to didactic instruction. While individual trials report
positive effects, the magnitude and certainty of benefit across outcome levels has not
been quantified in an RCT-only synthesis mapped to the New World Kirkpatrick Model (NWKM).

We therefore conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs comparing game-based
teaching with conventional teaching in nursing learners, classifying outcomes by NWKM level
(L1 reaction/engagement; L2 knowledge/skill/confidence; L3 clinical behaviour change;
L4 patient/system outcomes).

# Methods

## Eligibility criteria

**Designs:** RCTs and cluster-RCTs. **Intervention:** game-based teaching with explicit game
mechanics or a complete GBL/serious-game architecture. **Population:** nursing learners
(students, interns/trainees, clinical nurses, clinical nursing teachers). **Comparator:**
conventional teaching without game mechanics (lecture, case discussion, usual course,
self-study). **Outcome:** ≥1 quantitative learning/teaching outcome with comparable data.
Excluded: single-group pre/post; observational/cross-sectional/qualitative; no game element;
comparator also gamified; no quantitative/comparable data. No language, year, specialty, or
setting restriction.

## Information sources and search

Databases searched (inception–May 2026): **PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Europe PMC**. The protocol
also specifies CINAHL, Embase, ERIC, PsycINFO, Cochrane Library, and Chinese databases (Airiti/
華藝); these were **not retrievable in the current environment** (no API entitlement/connector)
and are flagged for a manual-export round. The search combined three concept blocks —
(game-based teaching) AND (nursing) AND (RCT design filter) — using controlled vocabulary
(MeSH/Emtree) and free-text terms (full strings in `02_search/round-01/queries.txt`).

## Study selection, data extraction, and dimension coding

Records were de-duplicated by DOI/PMID/title. Title/abstract screening and eligibility
assessment were performed by AI reviewer agents against the protocol, with liberal
("when in doubt, retain") screening. For each included study we coded seven characterisation
dimensions: participant type, game type, NWKM outcome level(s), clinical specialty,
intervention duration, delivery platform, and comparator type. Outcome statistics
(group means, SDs, sample sizes, or effect sizes) were extracted where reported in abstracts.

## Risk of bias and certainty

Risk of bias was assessed with **RoB 2** (five domains). Certainty of evidence was rated with
**GRADE** per NWKM outcome level (RCTs start at High, downgraded for risk of bias, inconsistency,
indirectness, imprecision, publication bias). Both were performed by a single AI reviewer on
abstract-level information and are provisional.

## Synthesis

For L2 (knowledge/skill) outcomes, standardized mean differences (**Hedges' g**, positive =
game-based superior) were pooled using a **DerSimonian–Laird random-effects** model implemented
in Python (R was unavailable). Heterogeneity was quantified with Q, τ², and I²; a 95% prediction
interval was computed. Publication bias was not formally tested (<10 pooled studies).

# Results

## Study selection

The search returned 640 records (PubMed 205, Scopus 292, Europe PMC 143); 325 duplicates were
removed, leaving 315 for screening. After title/abstract screening (199 excluded) and eligibility
assessment of 116 reports (28 excluded — comparator gamified 11, non-RCT design 9, wrong
population 6, no quantitative outcome 1, no game element 1), **88 studies were provisionally
included** (61 RCTs confirmed from abstract; 27 pending full-text confirmation). Five studies
provided extractable group statistics for meta-analysis (@fig-prisma).

![PRISMA 2020 flow diagram.](figures/prisma_flow.png){#fig-prisma width=78%}

## Characteristics of included studies

Included studies predominantly enrolled nursing students (73/88), used GBL (34), serious games
(29), or gamification (24), and targeted L2 learning outcomes (83 studies report an L2 outcome;
29 also report L1). Clinical content concentrated on general/basic nursing (36) and critical
care/CPR/medication safety (32). Delivery was mostly digital (50). Full counts are in
@tbl-dimensions and @fig-dimensions.

{{< include ../05_data_extraction/dimension_table.md >}}

: Dimension cross-tabulation of included studies (n = 88). {#tbl-dimensions}

![Included studies by dimension.](figures/dimension_bars.png){#fig-dimensions width=95%}

## Meta-analysis of L2 (knowledge/skill) outcomes

Across 5 RCTs with extractable data, game-based teaching improved L2 learning outcomes versus
conventional teaching: pooled **Hedges' g = 0.65 (95% CI 0.24–1.05), p = 0.002**. Heterogeneity
was substantial (**I² = 71%**, τ² = 0.14, Q = 13.9 on 4 df), and the **95% prediction interval
(−0.72 to 2.01)** included the null, indicating the true effect in a new setting remains uncertain
(@fig-forest).

![Forest plot: game-based vs conventional teaching, L2 learning outcomes (random-effects).](figures/forest_plot_L2.png){#fig-forest width=85%}

## Risk of bias

On abstract-based RoB 2, all pooled studies were rated *some concerns* overall (one *high*),
driven mainly by unverifiable allocation concealment and the infeasibility of participant
blinding in educational interventions (@fig-rob).

![Risk of bias (RoB 2) traffic-light plot for pooled studies (preliminary).](figures/rob2_traffic_light.png){#fig-rob width=80%}

# Discussion

This RCT-only synthesis suggests that game-based teaching produces a **moderate improvement in
nursing learners' knowledge and skills** (g ≈ 0.65) relative to conventional teaching, consistent
with active-learning theory and with broader health-professions education literature. Effects on
reaction/engagement (L1) were positive but not poolable here; behaviour change (L3) was sparse,
and **no eligible study reported patient/system (L4) outcomes** — a notable evidence gap.

The substantial heterogeneity (I² = 71%) and a prediction interval crossing the null mean the
benefit is **inconsistent across contexts**: game type, dose/duration, platform, and comparator
intensity plausibly modify effects and warrant subgroup/meta-regression analysis once more
studies have full-text data.

## Limitations

This is an **automated, abstract-derived** synthesis with important limitations:
(1) only 3 of the protocol's databases were searchable — **CINAHL and Chinese sources, which are
central to nursing evidence, are missing**; (2) screening, extraction, RoB 2, and GRADE were
**single-reviewer (AI), not dual human-verified**; (3) effect sizes came from **abstracts**, so
only 5 of 88 studies could be pooled and 27 await RCT confirmation; (4) pooling mixed knowledge
and skill measures within L2; (5) publication bias was not assessed. Accordingly, the pooled
estimate and certainty ratings should be read as a **provisional signal**, not a definitive result.

## Next steps before submission

Add CINAHL/華藝 (and Embase/Cochrane with valid credentials) in a round-02 search; obtain full
texts; perform **dual independent** screening, extraction, RoB 2, and GRADE; re-extract all
effect sizes; run subgroup (by NWKM level, game type) and sensitivity analyses; assess
publication bias if ≥10 studies; register the protocol (PROSPERO).

# Conclusion

Current RCT evidence indicates a moderate, positive but heterogeneous effect of game-based
teaching on nursing learners' knowledge and skills, at Low–Very low certainty. Game-based
strategies are a promising adjunct to nursing education, but stronger, full-text, dual-reviewed
evidence — especially on behaviour and patient-level outcomes — is needed.

# Data and code availability

All search outputs, screening/extraction decisions, analysis scripts, and figures are in the
project repository under `projects/game-based-learning-nursing-education/`.
